articles.title: Why India is sharing missile secrets with its private sector
articles.summary: New policy allows India’s private sector to produce advanced weaponry, supporting its goal of military self-sufficiency.
articles.body:
India has taken a major step towards opening one of its most sensitive areas of defence production to private companies.

Defence Minister Rajnath Singh approved the transfer of technologies developed by the state-run Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) for all conventional missile systems to Indian industry for domestic production, the country’s Ministry of Defence said on Tuesday.

The move marks a significant shift for the sector dominated by government-run firms and research laboratories. Private companies will be able to compete for the technology and production rights, subject to technical qualifications, certifications and other regulatory requirements, the ministry said.

The Narendra Modi-led government says the aim is to move missiles from development into mass production faster, increase domestic manufacturing and reduce India’s dependence on imports.

So, does India’s private defence industry have the capacity to manufacture sophisticated missile systems at the scale and reliability the military needs, is the country moving towards developing its own military-industrial complex, and are there security risks involved?

India’s Defence Ministry said Singh had approved the transfer of DRDO-developed technology for all conventional missile systems to Indian defence companies for production inside the country.

“The objective is to enhance domestic manufacturing capabilities, strengthen the defence industrial base, and create opportunities for the participation of Indian MSMEs (micro, small and medium-sized enterprises) and other technology partners in the supply chain,” the ministry said in a statement.

The measure would enable the “successful transition of missile system development to industrial production” and create opportunities for MSMEs and other technology partners, the ministry added.

“DRDO remains committed to working closely with Indian industry to facilitate the transfer and absorption of advanced defence technologies and to further strengthen the country’s indigenous defence capabilities.”

The announcement spans a wide range of missiles, said Aditya Ramanathan, a research fellow with the Bengaluru-based Takshashila Institution.

“It will include surface-to-air missiles, air-to-air missiles, anti-radiation missiles, antitank systems, and so on. It will also include more heavy-duty hardware like land-attack cruise missiles,” he told Al Jazeera.

India has traditionally relied heavily on state-owned defence companies to turn weapons developed by DRDO into large-scale production. Bharat Dynamics, one such state-owned company, has long held a monopoly in missile production.

Tuesday’s announcement is a “big change” because it ends that monopoly, said Ramanathan.

“Private companies have been making missile components for years, but what this decision does is allow them to move up the value chain and become prime integrators for these systems,” he said.

While India largely relies on domestically made missiles, it also imports missiles — especially from Russia and Israel, two key weapons suppliers to the country.

But under Modi, India has attempted to both encourage self-reliance in defence — a concept that the government calls Atmanirbhar Bharat or self-reliant India — and prod foreign defence majors to manufacture in India.

At a time when geopolitical allegiances are changing fast, and India faces uncertainties on both major borders — with rivals Pakistan and China — the country under Modi has more than doubled its defence budget, from $38bn in 2014 to $86bn in the current financial year.

The brief four-day conflict with nuclear-armed rival and neighbour Pakistan last year has injected fresh urgency into India’s defence preparedness plans. This year’s defence budget is 16 percent higher than the previous year’s.

Other geopolitical events have forced the government’s hand too, suggested Ramanathan.

“I don’t think this move would have happened as soon as it did if not for the experience of recent wars. Indian decision-makers have been looking at Ukraine, they’ve been looking at the US war with Iran, and of course they’ve been imbibing the lessons of operations from last year,” he said.

“One reason you’re going to need large stockpiles is that, as we’ve seen recently, you’re going to burn through your inventory pretty quickly. The other reason is that your adversary could also degrade your stockpiles using their own precision-strike systems.”

China, he said, was a major factor in India’s calculations.

“India believes that to deter China, which is its most capable adversary, it will need to demonstrate that it can both inflict and absorb really punishing attrition over weeks of gruelling warfare,” Ramanathan said.

To that end, India is also creating a tri-services conventional missile force. “To be a viable and effective force, it’s going to require serious magazine depth, and this cannot be achieved without the active involvement of the private sector,” he added.

What is India’s defence industry already manufacturing?

In June, India announced that it was preparing to spend more than $2bn on military drones from domestic manufacturers, reflecting the rapid expansion of the country’s private defence industry.

More than 600 companies were involved in India’s drone industry, including major groups such as Adani, Larsen & Toubro, and Tata Advanced Systems, as well as startups.

In July, India also approved the purchase of a range of military equipment for its defence forces worth $5.46bn, including missiles, electronic warfare systems and Kamikaze drones.

India is also pushing to rapidly modernise its navy with an eye on Beijing’s growing influence in key Indian Ocean shipping lanes. In December, New Delhi announced plans to procure at least 75 ships and submarines, with most expected to be constructed domestically.

At the same time, India is trying to diversify the foreign sources of its weapons. Over the past decade, New Delhi has worked to move away from its longstanding reliance on Russia for military hardware, expanding defence ties with countries such as the United States, France and — increasingly — Israel.

Does the private sector have the capacity to build missiles?

Private arms manufacturers in India have been increasing spending on bolstering military production in the past few years.

Major conglomerates have invested heavily in ammunition, drones, aerospace and military electronics. Of late, they have started to invest in facilities that aim to manufacture missiles.

Adani Defence & Aerospace, owned by business tycoon Gautam Adani, a close associate of Indian Prime Minister Modi, announced plans in 2024 to invest more than 30 billion rupees ($315m) in ammunition and missile manufacturing facilities in Uttar Pradesh.

The facilities would include capabilities for handling explosives used in missiles and precision munitions.

But commitments and intent don’t build missiles.

“Ultimately, I think the success or failure of this move will depend on how the Indian government places orders,” Ramanathan said. “Making missiles is an incredibly complex and costly affair, and companies are going to have to invest a lot in infrastructure, technology and people. These sorts of investments will only pay off if the government places large enough orders to justify them and also, hopefully, leave these companies with some profits that they can pour back into research and development.”

India has a range of cruise and ballistic missiles, several of which are also capable of carrying nuclear warheads.

In May, on the anniversary of the 2025 war with Pakistan, India successfully test-fired the Agni-V, its most advanced nuclear-capable intercontinental ballistic missile that can reach a distance of 5,500km (3,418 miles) — a range that covers all of China, the Middle East and even parts of Europe.

Its other ballistic missiles have ranges from as little as the Prithvi-1 (150km or 93 miles) to the Agni-IV (4,000km or 2,485 miles), again covering everything from border skirmishes with Pakistan to India’s extended neighbourhood.

It also has powerful cruise missiles, like the BrahMos, co-developed with Russia, which has a range of up to 500km (311 miles), and was used in last year’s war with Pakistan.

Is India also exporting missiles and other weapons?

India has dramatically ramped up its military exports in recent years, from just $72m in 2014-15 — when Modi came to power — to $4bn in 2025-2016.

Paras Defence, one of India’s fast-growing defence manufacturers, said this month it expects its exports to more than double in the 2026–27 financial year, up to $14m, driven partly by increased demand linked to conflicts in the Middle East.

Indian arms makers have also been involved in joint ventures with companies abroad. Adani Defence, in partnership with Elbit Systems – Israel’s largest weapons manufacturer – produces the large Hermes 900 armed drone systems.

A 2024 investigation by Al Jazeera exposed how India was exporting rocket parts and ammunition to Israel, even as the Modi government was publicly calling for diplomacy to end the war on Gaza.

In June 2026, Amnesty International said in a report that India’s weapons exports to Israel made it complicit in the genocide in Gaza.

But it isn’t just Israel that has sought and received weapons from Indian manufacturers. Nor is it just bullets and weapons parts that India is exporting today — complete missiles are in demand, too.

In 2022, the Philippines bought three batteries of the BrahMos missiles from India. Since then, Vietnam and Indonesia have signed deals with India for the purchase of these missiles. And India has submitted a proposal to the United Arab Emirates offering to supply the Gulf country these missiles, too.

Is the latest move a step towards building a military-industrial complex?

While Tuesday’s announcement marks the first time that India’s state-run research and manufacturing facilities will transfer missile technology to the private sector, the government earlier this year shortlisted private firms to manufacture the country’s next-generation fighter jets.

Tata Advanced Systems, a subsidiary of Tata Sons, and Bharat Forge are among companies to be shortlisted, and are emerging as major makers of artillery systems, ammunition and aerospace systems. India has its homegrown jets, but imports the most cutting-edge planes in its arsenal, including the Rafale fighters from France. The Indian Air Force also relies heavily on Soviet-era jets.

Still, while India “wants to build a wider defence industrial base”, said Ramanathan, “it is very far from developing the sort of military-industrial complex that [former US President Dwight] Eisenhower worried about. Power in India still resides overwhelmingly with the government.”

Despite the surge in domestic manufacturing and exports of specific weapons systems and parts, India on the whole remains a major military importer.

India was the world’s second-largest importer of weapons between 2021 and 2025, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI): Russia was its biggest source, accounting for 40 percent of India’s imported weapons.

Are there risks in transferring sensitive technology to the private sector?

As the US and Israel bombed Iran in March this year, a group of Iranian hackers claimed it broke into the servers of major US defence manufacturer Lockheed Martin, stealing blueprints of components used in the F-35 fighter jets.

The alleged data breach exposed the risks of private companies — which often have lower security standards and oversight than top-secret government laboratories — holding sensitive information.

But Ramanathan pointed out that in India’s case, “the companies that are most likely to get the missile contracts are all old hands”.

“They’ve been involved in the defence sector in some capacity for decades, and they have experience in dealing with confidentiality and secrecy,” he said.

The Indian government, on its part, also “doesn’t want the technology or its missile secrets to go to its adversaries, and it also wants to abide by its commitments to the Missile Technology Control Regime, which gives India several advantages,” he said, referring to one of the world’s major export-control regimes.

“So India has good reasons, in its own self-interest, to ensure that missile technology doesn’t leak.”

articles.title: In 1962, IBM built a secret NSA computer that ran jobs up to 200 times faster than any other machine; 14 years later a worn-out part ended its run because its maker was no longer in business
articles.summary: Tech News News: IBM built a secret computer for the US National Security Agency that began operating in 1962 and remained in service for 14 years, processing some of .
articles.body: IBM built a secret computer for the US National Security Agency that began operating in 1962 and remained in service for 14 years, processing some of the agency's most sensitive cryptographic workloads during the Cold War. Known as Harvest, the machine could run certain jobs up to 200 times faster than other computers of its time, according to accounts of its capabilities.According to a report by IEEE Spectrum, Harvest finally stopped running on February 27, 1976, after a mechanical component in its automated tape library wore out. The manufacturer of the part was no longer in business, leaving the NSA without a practical way to replace it. By then, the machine had operated through the Cuban Missile Crisis, the Vietnam War, and the period leading up to the 1975 Helsinki Accords.IBM built Harvest as a specialised NSA computerHarvest was officially designated the IBM 7950 and was built around IBM's 7030 Stretch mainframe. IBM developed Stretch for scientific computing, but the NSA needed a system that could continuously process large volumes of intercepted communications without requiring operators to manually stage each batch of tape.After two unsuccessful proposals, IBM secured the NSA contract in 1958. The resulting system combined Stretch with a custom streaming processor and an automated tape-storage system called Tractor.Unlike a general-purpose computer, Harvest's custom processor was designed to repeatedly apply a fixed sequence of operations to data streams. It could take two streams, known as P and Q, from memory, process them and return the result as a third stream, R.The processor used overlapping stages, or a pipeline, so that while one pair of data bytes was being processed, the next could already be fetched from memory. Harvest shared memory with Stretch and could address individual bits rather than being restricted to complete bytes or words.Its processing units included a logic unit for bitwise operations and a table-lookup unit that could use incoming data to address information in memory.Harvest processed large volumes of intercepted dataThe NSA used Harvest for cryptanalytic and large-scale text-processing jobs. One documented example described the machine searching 3.5 billion characters of text for any of 7,000 target terms in just under four hours.Another job, referred to as âMoretown,â involved searching 11 million messages covering 16 years of intercepted traffic against about 8,000 search terms. NSA analyst Robert Looney said in 1972 that the job took about 10 hours, although he did not disclose the purpose of the search.As a complete system, Harvest could stream one byte every 0.3 microseconds and had about 800 kilobytes of addressable memory.IBM engineer Frances Allen, who worked on both Stretch and Harvest, later recalled the type of operations the machine could perform.âIt was quite an amazing computer,â Allen said in a 2001 oral history. âOne instruction, for example, could do sorts, and do statistical analysis of the data that was streaming by it.â¦ Everything we were doing at that time was on the cutting edge. There was no question about it.âHarvest's specialised design also created challenges within the NSA. According to James Bamford's 2001 history of the agency, some officials reportedly looked at the machine during employee tours and said, âItâs beautiful, but it doesnât work.âThe system nonetheless continued to handle large jobs that general-purpose machines were not well suited to process.IBM built Tractor to keep Harvest supplied with dataHarvest's processing capacity required a storage system that could supply large datasets without constant human intervention. IBM therefore built Tractor, an automated magnetic-tape library officially designated the IBM 7955.Each Tractor cassette weighed about 6 to 7 kilograms and contained roughly 120 megabytes of data on a 550-metre reel of tape. Each storage unit could hold up to 160 cassettes.When Harvest began operating in 1962, three automatic cartridge units were connected to it, each serving two tape drives. Together, they provided about 44 gigabytes of online storage.The automated system used a motor-driven arm to retrieve cassettes from storage racks and deliver them to tape drives. The mechanism could move at about 6 metres per second, while software running on Stretch controlled cassette movement and data reading and writing.Moving from one completed tape to the next could take about 18 seconds, once the next cassette had been retrieved and was ready to mount. Retrieving and preparing a cassette did not require manual handling.Tractor therefore functioned as both long-term storage and a source of data for Harvest's processing jobs. Conventional reel-to-reel drives connected to Stretch were also used when large datasets had to be transferred into or out of the system.Harvest had its own programming languageIBM and the NSA also developed a programming language specifically for Harvest. Called Alpha, short for Advanced Language for Programming Harvest, it was designed around the machine's streaming architecture and the needs of cryptanalysts.Alpha allowed programmers to define the alphabet used for cryptographic data and included symbols for representing uncertain or null characters. A âscab,â represented by a question mark, indicated a character that was known to exist but whose identity was unknown. A blank space represented a âpad,â or null character.The language also provided ways to combine strings into larger structures, giving programmers a way to describe complex intercepted messages and cryptanalytic datasets.Allen worked on the Harvest software and later recalled that the technical report she produced for her part of the project disappeared into the NSA's classified system after she completed it.âI spent the good part of a summer on that,â she recalled in 2001. âAnd it just disappeared into Fort Meade somewhere.âHarvest's secrecy also shaped how some IBM employees understood the project. Allen said the NSA was not widely known outside classified intelligence circles when she began working on the machine, so she initially believed she was working on a naval project. The budget code name for the NSA was âBureau of Ships.âHarvest remained in use as newer computers arrivedBy 1971, Harvest was operating about 115 hours a week, according to Looney, representing more than two-thirds of its available operating time. At the same time, the number of jobs it handled had been declining since 1967 as newer general-purpose computers took over ordinary data-processing work.Harvest was increasingly reserved for large, specialised workloads that other machines could not handle as efficiently.At the system's 10th anniversary in 1972, Looney described it as a machine âconceived in the fifties, born in the sixties, and irreplaceable in the seventies.âThe description did not last much longer.On February 27, 1976, operators shut Harvest down for the final time. A mechanical component in the Tractor tape library had worn out, and the company that manufactured the part was no longer operating. Replacing the system's ageing hardware was no longer practical.The NSA marked the occasion with a mock telegram written in Harvest's name. âI first began operations at NSA. Although not widely known, I was probably the largest, fastest, and most technically advanced computer system in the world,â it said. âAnd now, fourteen years later, the time to retire has come. The cost of my upkeep and operation has been overtaken by more modern equipment and the newer technologies.âThe NSA replaced Harvest with the Cray-1The NSA eventually replaced Harvest with the Cray-1 supercomputer. Unlike Harvest, the Cray-1 used newer integrated circuits and was designed primarily for numerical and scientific computing, but its processing capabilities also made it suitable for workloads that had previously required Harvest's specialised hardware.The Cray-1 was also commercially available to multiple customers, unlike Harvest, which had been built specifically for the NSA. As newer general-purpose and scientific systems improved, maintaining a custom machine for one specialised workload became less practical.Harvest did not have a direct line of successors, partly because its architecture was built around the NSA's particular requirements. Several of its concepts, however, appeared later in other areas of computing.Tractor's automated tape library anticipated robotic storage systems later used in large data centres. Harvest's pipeline architecture also resembled approaches that became part of dataflow computing, while its continuous pattern-matching operations have parallels in later systems designed to inspect network traffic.Harvest's operational life ended with a worn mechanical part and an unavailable manufacturer, but the ideas used to build the system continued to appear in computing systems developed after it.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: A New Zealand sailor spent years living alone on a remote Cook Islands atoll across three separate stays; a year after his final stay ended, Suwarrow was declared a national park
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A remote Pacific atoll that was once the solitary kingdom of a New Zealand sailor has secured a lasting future, transforming from a hermit's retreat i.
articles.body: A remote Pacific atoll that was once the solitary kingdom of a New Zealand sailor has secured a lasting future, transforming from a hermit's retreat into the first conservation sanctuary in the Cook Islands. Suwarrow, an isolated coral atoll about 1,300 kilometres north of Rarotonga, was officially declared a national park in 1978. The decision came just one year after its most famous resident, Tom Neale, ended his final stay on the island. Neale spent about 16 years living as a solitary beachcomber on Anchorage Island, the main islet in the Suwarrow atoll. His life there, described in his 1966 autobiography An Island to Oneself, turned the tiny island into a symbol of complete isolation. Today, government records and historical archives document how the remote retreat became an important environmental reserve.A life of deliberate isolationBorn in Wellington, New Zealand, in 1902, Neale joined the Royal New Zealand Navy as a young man before buying out his contract to travel independently around the Pacific. He later worked on several islands as a trader and storekeeper. He eventually met American author Robert Dean Frisbie, whose stories about Suwarrow inspired Neale to seek a quiet life on the remote atoll. Neale first visited Suwarrow in 1945 while delivering supplies to wartime coast-watchers. He was fascinated by the small ring of coral and spent years getting permission and gathering supplies to live there. In October 1952, Neale arrived on the uninhabited atoll with two cats, a radio, tools and basic supplies. He lived there during three separate periods: from 1952 to 1954, 1960 to 1963, and 1967 to 1977. During his stays, he repaired abandoned huts, grew vegetables, raised chickens and relied mainly on fish, breadfruit and coconut crabs for food.Explaining why he chose to leave modern society behind, Neale wrote in his autobiography: "I chose to live in the Pacific islands because life there moves at the sort of pace which you feel God must have had in mind originally when He made the sun to keep us warm and provided the fruits of the earth for the taking." His isolated life was eventually brought to an end by health problems. He suffered a serious back injury during his first stay and was diagnosed with stomach cancer during his final period on the island. He left Suwarrow for good in March 1977 and died in Rarotonga later that year at the age of 75.From remote retreat to national parkAfter Neale's departure and death, the Cook Islands government moved to protect the natural environment of the atoll he had called home. In 1978, the entire atoll, its surrounding reef and a six-kilometre marine area were declared the country's first national park and bird sanctuary. Official environmental records maintained by the National Library of New Zealand and the Cook Islands National Environment Service describe Suwarrow as an important ecological sanctuary. Protecting the atoll as a park helped shield its fragile habitats from commercial development and uncontrolled exploitation. The Cook Islands National Environment Service also maintains strict rules for the area. Visitors need permission to enter, while vessels must obtain permits before arriving.A haven for wildlifeAlthough Neale made Suwarrow famous among sailors and readers around the world, the atoll's greatest value lies in its wildlife. The reef system includes 30 small islets, or motus, surrounding a sheltered central lagoon. Together, they form one of the important seabird breeding areas in the South Pacific. Regional environmental surveys show that Suwarrow supports roughly nine per cent of the world's Lesser Frigatebird population. It also has important breeding colonies of Red-tailed Tropicbirds and Sooty Terns. The surrounding waters support coconut crabs, green sea turtles and several shark species. To protect these animals, the national park is left without permanent human habitation for part of the year. From November to March, during the Pacific cyclone season, people are not allowed to stay on the atoll, giving wildlife a period with little human disturbance.Neale's legacy on Anchorage IslandMore than four decades after Neale's final departure, signs of his life remain on Anchorage Island. The small wooden hut he repaired and lived in has been preserved by seasonal park caretakers. Part of it has been turned into a small lending library for sailors and passing yachtsmen. A concrete bust of the New Zealand sailor also stands nearby as a tribute to his remarkable life. Today, two caretakers stay on the island during the dry season. They manage visitors, monitor bird populations and help protect the fragile environment. Neale came to Suwarrow in search of solitude and a simple life. His story, however, helped bring international attention to the remote atoll and its natural beauty. What began as one man's private escape from modern society eventually became a protected sanctuary designed to keep the island's wildlife and wilderness intact for generations. A closer look at Tom Neale's extraordinary life on Suwarrow can be found in the archival documentary Tom Neale: Man Who Lived Alone on a Remote Island. The footage provides historical context on Neale's daily life, his survival on Anchorage Island and the years he spent living alone in one of the Pacific's most isolated corners.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Islamabad PIMS hospital fire: Witnesses say rescue was delayed as blaze killed 14 babies
articles.summary: A hospital official told the BBC that the door to the ward was not locked, but manned with security guards, to protect the babies.
articles.body:
It was just after dawn on Wednesday morning at a maternity ward in the Pakistani capital when a horrific blaze erupted.

It would go on to kill 14 infants as parents say they waited hours for help to arrive.

Hivsa Walid was near the room at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) hospital with her sister-in-law, who had given birth days earlier. She initially heard a shout and thought a patient had died - but then she saw smoke.

The pair fled with the baby, who is so small she does not yet have a name.

"We didn't even think about our belongings. We just grabbed the baby and rushed downstairs.

"Some patients had delivered their babies just that night. I don't even know how we managed to get down - it was all a blur."

The fire broke out in an air-conditioning unit on the third floor of the mother and child unit at PIMS, one of the main state-run hospitals in Islamabad. Only one of the 15 babies present was saved.

Khurram Mehmood, 40, told AFP news agency there was a long wait for rescue workers. "I lost my daughter. She was only three days old," he said.

Jaweria, the mother of another victim, told AFP news agency the door to the maternity ward was locked.

"For two hours I kept crying and wailing," she said. "Police arrived after four hours and said they are here to investigate."

"Why did the doctors leave the children there?" she asks.

"To hell with you, rescue team and police. Babies burnt to death there, but nobody could save them."

Rana Imran Sikander, the hospital's executive director, told the BBC the ward's door was not locked but was manned. He cited the need to protect babies from being stolen, something that has happened before at government hospitals.

Walid suggested PIMS's safety protocols were inadequate, despite it being a major hospital. "There should have been fire extinguishers and protocols, but no one was doing anything - everyone was just running."

The father of a baby who died told Reuters he had been visiting the ward for eight days and the building had "no fire security, no proper exits".

"All doors were closed, only one door was for us to visit our children. They kept the other doors locked because they feared we would come to see our children too often."

Several eyewitnesses have claimed duty staff were not around.

People had to "break the door down" and rescue teams were forced to smash the windows to control the flames, a witness who did not give her name told AFP.

Abdul Ghafoor, another witness, told AFP he tried to get into the building to rescue patients but couldn't reach the maternity ward.

"There was thick black smoke inside and patients were trapped," he said. "Rescue teams arrived after almost two hours."

Islamabad's Chief Commissioner Sohail Ashraf has said rescue teams reached the scene "immediately" after the emergency call was first made, according to AFP.

PIMS is one of the biggest hospitals in Pakistan's capital, with 156 beds in its maternal and child health unit.

Pakistan has dealt with a number of major fires in recent years, with poor safety laws, building codes and lax enforcement often blamed for steep death tolls.

Survivors of a fire which killed dozens at a Karachi shopping mall in January this year said locked exits likely contributed to the high number of fatalities.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has expressed his "deep sorrow and heartfelt regret" over the latest blaze, and instructed authorities to "conduct an immediate investigation", according to a statement from his office.

He has also suspended Federal Health Secretary Aslam Ghauri, a top official in the health department.

"Such a situation with children is irreparable", the statement said.

articles.title: Sark could protect 30% of waters in marine plan
articles.summary: The proposal would give added protection to about 50 sq miles (128.8 sq km) of sea around Sark.
articles.body:
An island wants to protect 30% of its waters under plans aimed at safeguarding marine life.

The proposal would see about 50 sq miles (128.8 sq km) of sea around Sark in the Channel Islands receive additional protection under plans developed by the island's agriculture, environment and sea fisheries committee with support from the Blue Marine Foundation, local fishermen and marine experts.

Freddie Watson, Channel Islands project manager at Blue Marine Foundation, told BBC Radio Guernsey that marine protection could help safeguard sensitive habitats while supporting sustainable fishing.

The proposal is expected to be submitted to the island's governing Chief Pleas by 1 September.

Watson explained that evidence had been used to identify important habitats, including previously unmapped areas of seagrass, so protection could be focused where it was needed most.

The waters around Sark are home to species including European spiny lobster, rays, catsharks, octopus and pink sea fans.

Watson said the plans formed part of a wider effort across the Channel Islands to safeguard marine environments, including a plan to protect more than 20% of Jersey's waters.

Watson said stronger protection could bring benefits for both wildlife and people by helping to sustain fish stocks and preserve habitats that support marine biodiversity.

He added: "Some of those habitats are really important at drawing down and locking away carbon."

The Sark proposal depends on political approval, with members of Chief Pleas expected to debate the plans on 30 September.

articles.title: Iran, Oman agree on temporary Hormuz route: What we know
articles.summary: Iran’s deputy foreign minister announced a temporary shipping corridor in the Strait of Hormuz.
articles.body:
Iran and Oman have agreed on a temporary maritime route for ships travelling through the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said on Tuesday.

He, however, warned that the waterway will not fully reopen until the United States fulfils its commitments under an interim peace deal signed in June, which has since lapsed.

The US-Israel war on Iran, which began with strikes on Tehran on February 28, has effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz to shipping, sending global energy markets into crisis. The narrow waterway through which one-fifth of global oil and natural gas supplies from Gulf producers are shipped in peacetime has become a major bone of contention between Washington and Tehran, and disagreements over the critical channel continue to hinder any hopes of a lasting peace plan.

Since the US bombing of parts of Iran in July following more disputes over the strait, Iran has refused to hold direct talks with it. Even though active warfare has since paused again – replaced by a strategy of piling economic pressure on Iran – it has maintained that it will speak directly to only Oman about the future of the waterway, which passes through the territorial waters of the two countries.

Here is what we know about the new route they have agreed on.

Before the war on Iran began, more than 20 percent of global oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) shipments from the regional producers passed through the strait, which is the only sea route connecting the Gulf to the open ocean. About 130 ships crossed the strait every day. Just before the war began, the price of Brent crude – the global benchmark for oil – was about $66 a barrel.

Following the attacks on Tehran, which were carried out as talks between Iran and the US were underway in Oman, Iran closed the strait in early March, allowing only a few ships it deemed “friendly” to pass through. In April, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) issued a route map to those ships allowed to pass. This routed traffic much closer to the Iranian coast than they had previously sailed and designated a large section of Omani territorial waters as “restricted”.

The US has previously accused Iran of placing mines in the strait. While Iran has not confirmed this, it stated at the time that following its designated route would minimise the risk of encountering them.

Below is a map of the route approved by Iran in April:

The US later enforced a naval blockade of Iranian ports in and around the strait in a bid to cripple the country by restricting its fuel exports.

The war and ensuing regional tensions resulted in global energy shortages, especially in Asia where countries are particularly dependent on shipments from the Gulf, and crude prices soared. Over the course of the war, the price surged past $100 on several occasions, most recently on July 23. In March, the highest Brent crude oil price reached almost $120 a barrel.

On June 17, a memorandum of understanding (MoU) was signed between the US and Iran as they agreed to a ceasefire to facilitate peace negotiations, lasting up to 60 days. Among other measures, Iran agreed to keep the strait open for all traffic, free of charge, for 60 days. However, the vague wording of the MoU led to disagreements over which routes ships should take and the waterway fractured into two disputed routes – a southern course approved by Oman and backed by the US, and a northern one approved by Iran. The southern route is the one used by commercial carriers under US naval protection so far.

Diplomatic efforts towards a broader peace deal have since stalled and passage through the strait remains high risk.

On Tuesday, an oil tanker was disabled by an unidentified projectile close to Oman’s Ash Shishah, near the strait’s entrance, the United Kingdom’s Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said.

On Tuesday, Gharibabadi announced on state television that Iran and Oman have agreed that the entry to the new approved route will begin in Iranian territorial waters “and part of the exit route would also be through our territorial waters”.

The transit corridor will be 7 miles (11.3km) wide, he said.

However, key details remain unclear, including the precise coordinates of the route, when ships can start traversing the strait safely and how revenues would be generated.

Specific operational protocols are also not known yet, such as whether any vessels or flags will be barred from using the route.

Does this mean the Strait of Hormuz will reopen?

No. Gharibabadi emphasised that Iran has only agreed on a route for shipping with Oman, and does not consider the strait open despite the agreement on the location of a shipping route with Oman.

“The agreed-upon transit route with Oman is a temporary route,” he added.

Iranian army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia said vessels will be subject to Iranian surveillance before they enter the strait and will only be allowed to pass if Iran grants them permission.

Gharibabadi insisted the US must fulfil its commitments under the June MoU, including granting sanctions relief and the release of frozen Iranian assets, if it wants to resume peace talks.

He urged countries to resist US pressure to place economic pressure on Iran.

US President Donald Trump announced last week the “most crushing economic operation ever” against Iran, and threatened sanctions against any country doing business with it . On Monday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent laid out a wave of new sanctions against 60 entities around the world it accuses of facilitating Iranian oil sales.

“We are urging countries not to succumb to American pressure regarding the sanctions that Washington wants to impose on us,” Gharibabadi said, adding that Washington was “mistaken about its ability to enforce its sanctions against our neighbours”.

Gharibabadi’s remarks followed talks with Omani negotiators in Tehran to finalise the details of a phased framework for the future management of the strait. Iran and Oman have been in talks for several weeks about controlling traffic through the strategic waterway.

Oman, which is known for its neutrality and position as a mediator between Iran and the US, which it considers an ally, has not publicly stated that it intends to join Iran in controlling the Strait of Hormuz.

Earlier on Tuesday, Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met his Omani counterpart, Badr Albusaidi, in Tehran to discuss the temporary navigation corridor as well as a project to clear mines, according to a joint statement.

Albusaidi said on X he hoped the countries would “soon announce” the corridor, adding that “future management of the strait and a permanent solution will follow in due course”.

Technical talks are planned to develop a long-term arrangement, including mechanisms for information sharing and navigational and security services, according to Albusaidi’s statement.

While the US has not formally responded to the news of an agreement between Iran and Oman for a shipping passage through the strait, last week Trump threatened to bomb Oman if it “gets in the way” of a peace deal between the US and Iran.

“If Oman gets in the way, we’ll bomb the s*** out of them,” he told US broadcaster Fox News on August 17. Back in May, he made a similar threat , saying, “Nobody is going to control it. It’s international waters, and Oman will behave just like everybody else, or we will have to blow them up.”

Trump also told Fox that Iran should surrender, and claimed that his administration had opened a direct backchannel for talks with the IRGC, something Iranian officials immediately denied.

On Wednesday, an IRGC spokesman told Iranian media that the US has been obstructing negotiations between Oman and Iran, leading to them being delayed.

The US and Oman are close partners with a relationship stretching back nearly 200 years.

However, an exclusive understanding between Iran and Oman over the waterway runs contrary to one of Washington’s core demands: that Iran should relinquish control of the strait as a condition of ending the war. Rather than curbing that control, such a deal would lend it greater legitimacy by formalising Iran’s position, analysts say.

But experts say Trump is also likely angry that the US has seemingly been cut out of a deal relating to the strait.

“In part, a solution mediated without US intervention and which in fact allows Oman and Iran to manage passage through Hormuz, which lies entirely within the two countries’ territorial waters, would show how impotent the United States is and has been,” Laleh Khalili, a professor of Gulf studies at the University of Exeter in the UK, told Al Jazeera last week.

The US and Iran have also strongly disagreed about whether Iran should be allowed to charge fees to shipping companies using the strait. Under international law, tolls for passing through natural waterways such as Hormuz are forbidden, even when they are not technically in international waters. However, fees for services such as insurance, environmental protection and docking can be charged. It has yet to be seen whether this issue will be addressed in the temporary agreement announced on Tuesday.

The US has long accused Iran of planting sea mines – explosives planted underwater to threaten commercial and military ships – in the Strait of Hormuz. Sea mines can include moored contact mines that detonate when a vessel strikes them, while more sophisticated “bottom mines” sit on the seabed and use sensors to trigger an explosion when they detect a ship’s magnetic or acoustic signature above.

There is no clear answer as to how many mines there are or where exactly the sea mines are in Hormuz, as Iran has not officially disclosed this. Trump has asserted that US forces have destroyed “all” 28 Iranian mine-laying boats in the strait’s international waters.

On Tuesday, Gharibabadi dismissed Trump’s claim, saying it was “only aimed at calming the markets”. He warned that US mine-detection vessels would become “very good targets” if they entered the area.

articles.title: Farmers in Jersey urge people to 'be patient' amid drought
articles.summary: Farmers and animal charities says summer heatwaves have had a "huge impact" on crops.
articles.body:
Farmers and animal charities say this summer's heatwaves and droughts have had a "huge impact" on crops and feed.

Meteorologists have said summer 2026 is on course to be the Channel Islands' hottest since records began , with temperatures reaching as high as 39.3C (102.74F) in Jersey in June before it was later declared in drought .

Clairval Organic Dairy Farm near Maufant said in a post on social media the weather was "tough" for growers and dairy farmers and staff were urging people to "be patient" about supplies and prices.

Rebecca Hefford, owner of animal charity Paws and Claws, in St Mary, said "it's been very difficult" and the predicted hotter summers would be a "disaster" for farmers.

Clairval said grass was no growing as it should, crops had not produced what they needed and fields needed reseeding.

The farm said there was not enough food available and the cost of it had gone "through the roof."

It said lots of steady, soaking rain over a sustained period was required to replenish the ground so things would start growing again.

"Understand that when food prices rise or things aren't quite as plentiful as they normally are, there are some very real reasons behind it.

"It's not easy being a farmer right now - we're doing our best to keep going, keep producing, and keep providing - but we need a little understanding along the way."

Hefford said the charity normally grew fruit and vegetables to help feed the animals in its care, but the drought had made that "virtually impossible'.

The charity cares for a variety of animals, including 132 birds of many varieties, including cockatiels and budgies; a horse, cats, tortoises and guinea pigs.

Hefford said the climate had made it very hard to feed the animals.

She said the average yearly spend on food was about £3,500, but she had spent about £4,500 so far this year.

articles.title: Glenwood Earl Pysher IV identified as 22-year-old killed in Montgomery County police shooting
articles.summary: A 22-year-old man who was shot and killed in an officer-involved shooting in Upper Pottsgrove Township has been identified by the Montgomery County District Attorney’s Office.
articles.body: A 22-year-old man who was shot and killed in an officer-involved shooting in Upper Pottsgrove Township has been identified by the Montgomery County District Attorney’s Office. According to prosecutors, Glenwood Earl Pysher IV was shot and killed by an Upper Pottsgrove Township police officer after a 911 call reported a possible break-in at a home on Snyder Road at around 12:29 a.m. on Sunday, Aug. 23. According to officials, police found a man behind the house when they arrived. Officials said an “encounter” followed, and police shot and killed Pysher. Erin Pysher, Glenwood’s mother, said that her son went to the wrong backyard by mistake and thought it was his friends house. She claimed that he was on the phone with friends for two minutes and then he was shot. “It’s a small little error that it cost him his life. It should’ve never happened,” she said. “The cops should have never resorted to such force. He was unarmed. He wasn’t trying to do anything dangerous or malicious or hurt anybody. It escalated way too fast.” Pysher had previously played as a baseball player for Northampton County Community College and had transferred to St. Elizabeth College in New Jersey for his senior season, where he was going to continue to play baseball and study to become a history teacher, his mother said. “He just turned 22 on the 10th. He just had a birthday he was supposed to start school and go to college. He was supposed to play baseball and live his life and it was cut short,” she said. The district attorney’s office said it is continuing to investigate the incident, and it will provide an update when it is completed.

articles.title: How Hegseth's 'purge' triggered a US Army leadership crisis as Iran war nears six months
articles.summary: International News: A leadership vacuum has opened up at the very top of the United States Army. This at a time when the US Army is actively engaged in West Asia, fightin.
articles.body: A leadership vacuum has opened up at the very top of the United States Army. This at a time when the US Army is actively engaged in West Asia, fighting off Iranian missiles and drones with its Patriot and THAAD air defence systems. This critical void , according to a report in the New York Times, is caused by a series of firings and internal feuds triggered by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth leaving the world's most powerful land force without a permanent chief of staff for months. This even as it grapples with a punishing drone and missile campaign against American bases in the Middle East. The New York Times reports that the Army has had no chief of staff since Hegseth abruptly removed General Randy George in April without any explanation. The report states that there is little indication that a replacement for the top US Army position is imminent.According to officials cited by the newspaper, Hegseth has since pushed out at least three senior officers who had been seen as strong contenders to succeed General George, effectively narrowing the Army's leadership pipeline at a moment when continuity at the top matters most, as the force is moving towards more autonomous systems, which requires changes institutionally, doctrinally and structurally. These changes are informed by the change in the nature of combat in both Ukraine, where the US Army is providing intelligence and in West Asia, where it is deployed actively.The report also states that army secretary Daniel Driscoll, the service's senior most civilian official, is also expected to exit the administration in the coming months and has reportedly already begun moving out of his office, adding to the sense of institutional drift. In total, current and former officials suggest Hegseth has forced out roughly half a dozen senior officers since taking charge, a churn that insiders say has eroded expertise at the army's highest ranks.The scale of the shake-up becomes clearer when set against historical numbers. When Hegseth assumed office in January last year, the US Army had ten four-star generals, that number has now fallen to just five, the fewest the service has fielded in decades, according to the report. It also states that Secretary of War Hegseth was forced to leave the Army National Guard, after he was flagged as an 'insider threat' member of the organisation.The timing could hardly be more consequential. American bases across West Asia have come under sustained attack from cheap, expendable Iranian drones since late February, a campaign that has already claimed the lives of at least eighteen US servicemembers and left many more wounded. Against this backdrop, critics argue that removing experienced commanders at precisely the moment the army needs steady, battle-tested leadership risks compounding an already difficult operational picture, leaving key modernisation and readiness decisions in the hands of an institution that, for now, effectively has no one steering from the top.

articles.title: ‘Lake America’? Who is responsible for naming geographic places?
articles.summary: President Donald Trump announced his desire to change the name amid an escalating trade dispute with Canada.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Amid an escalating trade dispute with Canada, President Trump has suggested that he could rename Lake Ontario to “Lake America.”

It isn’t the first time the president has decided to change a body of water to reflect his personal priorities and disputes with other countries. On the first day of his second term, Trump signed an order renaming the Gulf of Mexico to the “Gulf of America.”

But who actually determines the names for geographic features?

The job falls to the U.S. Board on Geographic Names (BGN), an organization created in 1890 and codified in its current form in 1947. The board’s function is to ensure uniform usage of geographic names within the federal government.

It originated during a time when a surge of expansion and mining led to inconsistencies in names that caused issues for surveyors, mapmakers and scientists who rely on standard names for clarity.

Over time, the BGN expanded to include the names of foreign countries and other areas of interest, standardizing the language the U.S. government uses.

As with most federal organizations, there’s bureaucracy involved. The process for submitting a name change involves a detailed proposal process and review.

The BGN enacted an official name change for the Gulf of America following the president’s executive order, starting a process to update maps, tools and federal documents.

But just because the U.S. declares a name change doesn’t mean it will be recognized elsewhere. The organization may have rechristened the Gulf of America, but much of the international community still uses the Gulf of Mexico.

The U.S. isn’t the only country to issue a name change that isn’t universally adopted. The U.S. government still refers to the country of Burma , which changed its name to Myanmar in 1989.

Nor is the nation alone in changing names amid larger disagreements . Conflicts over territory or national politics can lead to competing names, such as China’s South China Sea, which Vietnam calls the Eastern Sea and the Philippines the West Philippine Sea.

Similarly, the international community refers to the Persian Gulf, while Arab countries in the region use the Arabian Gulf.

Whether Trump pursues his effort to rename Lake Ontario remains to be seen.

articles.title: Photos: Avalanche floods kill eight, hundreds missing in Nepal’s Himalayas
articles.summary: Flash floods devastate Nepal’s Himalayas, washing away villages and infrastructure along the Bhotekoshi river.
articles.body:
Hundreds of people are missing and at least eight have been killed after an avalanche of ice and rock triggered massive flash floods in Nepal’s Himalayan region, washing away villages and infrastructure along the Bhotekoshi river.

Officials said 384 tourists, including 291 foreigners from India, Malaysia, the United Kingdom and the United States, were unaccounted for after Wednesday’s disaster, which struck at about 9am (03:15 GMT). Roads and hydropower projects were destroyed, and authorities issued alerts urging residents in several districts to keep away from the Bhotekoshi, Trishuli and Narayani rivers.

“We have asked both India and China to help us with the rescue efforts,” government spokesperson Sasmit Pokharel said.

Rasuwa district was worst hit, echoing similar flash floods in August last year when an overflowing glacial lake in neighbouring Tibet killed nine people and damaged a key cross-border bridge.

Climate experts at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development said an ice-rock avalanche on the Nepal side blocked the Lhende Khola, a Bhotekoshi tributary, before releasing a sudden surge downstream, underscoring growing risks in the rapidly warming Himalayas.

articles.title: Prince Harry and Meghan arrive back in UK, six years after leaving royal life behind
articles.summary: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex arrived back in the United Kingdom on Wednesday, multiple media outlets reported, six years after they left the country on stepping back from royal life.
articles.body: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex arrived back in the United Kingdom on Wednesday, multiple media outlets reported, six years after they left the country on stepping back from royal life. The BBC, the country’s public broadcaster, earlier reported that Prince Harry and Meghan – along with their two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet – were understood to have flown privately into Britain from California. The Telegraph newspaper reported the family landed around lunchtime on Wednesday at Birmingham Airport. CNN has reached out to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex. The Sussexes’ return to the UK after living in the United States for the past six years was revealed last week. Archie, 7, and Lilibet, 5, are already enrolled in British schools for the coming term, which is due to start in September. Harry and Meghan are returning to the UK as private citizens and will not be resuming any official duties on behalf of King Charles III. The couple left the UK for North America in 2020 after stepping back from royal life, and the years since have seen a public falling out with the wider royal family. Harry and Meghan had cited tabloid intrusion, racism in British institutions, online abuse and complex family dynamics as among the reasons behind their departure. Harry has made several trips back to the UK, including for the funeral of his grandmother Queen Elizabeth II in 2022 and the coronation of his father King Charles III the following year. Security sticking point The family were most recently back in Britain over the summer when they visited King Charles and Queen Camilla at Highgrove, the monarch’s private country residence in Gloucestershire, England. It was the first time the 77-year-old monarch had been reunited with his grandchildren in four years. The Sussexes also spent time with Harry’s mother’s side of the family at Althorp House, the Spencer estate in Northamptonshire. King Charles was only informed of the family’s move earlier this month. Prince William and Catherine, Princess of Wales were also told of the Sussexes’ plans. When asked by CNN last week why they were moving back, a source close to the couple would only remark on how much they enjoyed their visit as a family to the UK last month. Any time Prince Harry has previously returned to the UK, one sticking point has been his family’s close police protection. He has fought a yearslong legal battle against the UK government as his taxpayer-funded security was downgraded by its Royal and VIP Executive Committee (RAVEC) after he and Meghan ceased official work on behalf of the monarch. Since then, it has been determined on a case-by-case basis. Last year, he lost a challenge against the Home Office in the UK Court of Appeal on the decision. At the time, the duke said he couldn’t “see a world in which I would bring my wife and children back to the UK at this point.” It’s unclear if the security arrangements had changed in recent weeks or who would pay for any required security once back in Britain. At the end of June, he was still waiting on a review by RAVEC’s Risk Management Board. A UK government spokesperson has previously described its protective security system as “rigorous and proportionate.” Britain's Prince Harry and his wife Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, are among the most famous couples in the world.Harry, the second son of King Charles III and the late Princess Diana, was introduced to Meghan, an American actress, by mutual friends in 2016. They were married in 2018 in a ceremony watched by millions of people around the world.The two had their first child, Archie, in 2019. They had their second, Lilibet, in 2021.In January 2020, the couple announced that they would be stepping back from their roles as senior members of the British royal family, with a plan to work toward becoming "financially independent."They have lived in the United States for the past few years, but they are planning to move back to Britain, CNN understands. Harry and Meghan are said to be planning to relocate later this month to a private residence outside London, and they reportedly have enrolled their children in British schools for the coming term, according to UK newspaper The Telegraph. Separately in July, Harry and six other high-profile figures lost their privacy case against a British tabloid publisher in the UK High Court. Last week, a judge ruled that the group – which also includes Elton John and his husband David Furnish, must make an initial payment of £9.5 million ($13 million) to Associated Newspapers Limited. However, the group face paying up to a reported £34.5 million ($46.9 million) in total legal costs. Harry and Meghan are settling back in the UK for an extended period of time, according to British media, and will live in a private property outside of London. The pair have not yet spoken publicly about their plans. The duke will likely have charity engagements in the weeks ahead, such as the annual ceremony run by WellChild, a charity that cares for seriously ill children and young people in the UK. Preparations are also underway for his Invictus Games, which will be hosted in Birmingham next year. Meanwhile, Meghan’s latest posts on Instagram suggest she will continue to grow her As Ever lifestyle business.

articles.title: GTA 6 leaks: Rockstar issues statement over online clips
articles.summary: The game developer says the unauthorised footage has caused "heartbreak" for those working on the title.
articles.body:
Grand Theft Auto 6 maker Rockstar Games has issued a statement addressing a series of leaked videos showing the upcoming blockbuster video game.

Clips appearing to show gameplay and cinematics from the title began appearing online last week, but the developer did not acknowledge them straight away.

In a statement, the company said the leaks had been "heartbreaking" for the team working on the sequel, and that they were "not how we intended for you to see the game after all this time".

The company apologised for the delays in releasing official updates on the highly anticipated title, but vowed to "exceed" fans' expectations in a special preview airing on Netflix this week.

When leaks first began to surface, there was some doubt as to whether they were genuine.

But as the days went on, evidence mounted to suggest they were legitimate.

Copies of clips were quickly taken down from social media sites via copyright strikes, where the owner of a work can request its removal.

And, on Friday, Rockstar's parent company Take Two Interactive launched legal proceedings regarding the leaks in a New York court.

Rockstar acknowledged players had been waiting for it to address the leaked footage, and said it was "unfortunate the intended game experience may now be impacted by some spoilers".

It also thanked fans who sent messages of support over the past week, adding: "Your words have meant more to the team than you can imagine."

The group behind the leaks claims to be acting in the interests of players, accusing Rockstar of engaging in anti-consumer practices such as its decision not to release a disc version of GTA 6 at launch .

Not everyone is convinced, as each release of new material has invited viewers to send cryptocurrency "donations" to the user uploading them.

GTA 6, due to be released on PlayStation 5 and Xbox consoles in November, is still expected to be the biggest video game launch of the decade.

The previous game in the series, GTA 5, also broke records when it came out in 2013 and has sold more than 200 million copies since.

Two official trailers for the sixth game have almost 500 million combined views on YouTube, and the Netflix "extended look" on Thursday is being marketed as an event by the streaming service.

Next month the company is due to appear at an employment tribunal in Scotland to defend itself against claims it illegally sacked a group of ex-employees for trying to form a union .

It strongly denies the accusations, and says the workers were fired on the grounds of gross misconduct.

articles.title: Russia’s baiting and switching Latin Americans to fight its war
articles.summary: They were promised the moon and the stars but found only hell in a foreign land.
articles.body:
Russia seems to be losing the war in Ukraine , both morally and militarily. It was not a quick special operation. It has been a long and costly invasion, in which the Russians have had to seek out mercenaries in foreign countries, including Latin America.

In Mexico , Russia has recruited soldiers through social media platforms such as Facebook. Recruits are offered a $3,000 payment, accommodations, meals and a $28,000 bonus. Mexican authorities have confirmed 14 successful recruitments, although there could be many more.

But all that glitters is not gold. Job offers aimed at attracting potential recruits targeted construction and private security sectors. But upon arrival in Moscow , the plans changed: Their passports were confiscated. They were issued uniforms and sent to the front lines. The promised benefits and wages never materialized.

According to one estimate, since 2024, approximately 1,200 Peruvian citizens have enlisted in the Russian army. The vast majority received offers for jobs in kitchen services, security and transport. The package included a $2,500 monthly salary, accommodation and a bonus ranging from $20,000 to $50,000 .

Colombia has also been targeted by Russian recruitment efforts. After years from guerrilla warfare, terrorism and paramilitary violence, the nation has now a large population of impoverished, unemployed former combatants. They were the perfect target for Russian promises of a better life.

Offers circulating on social media and through word-of-mouth promised a monthly salary of $3,500, a $35,000 bonus and Russian citizenship. None of these promises are ever kept. As always, the Russian government denied any knowledge of these illicit operations, which were being repeated time and again.

Cases have also been reported in El Salvador , involving individuals who traveled to Russia seeking work, a good salary and other lucrative employment incentives. They received none of this; instead, they were sent to the front lines in Ukraine.

In Bolivia , Russia recruited impoverished individuals with similar offers and bonuses ranging from $16,000 to $20,000. Nearly 20 cases have been reported in Santa Cruz. The jobs targeted masons, plumbers, cooks and security guards. They were promised the moon and the stars but found only hell in a foreign land.

Russia has been using Cuban mercenaries since 2023 . The island’s soldiers are familiar with the weapons. They are both trained and paid cheaply, reducing Putin’s political cost to zero. No one in Moscow will complain about the deaths of foreign soldiers.

In 2025, Cuba took things to a new level. The number of Cuban mercenaries sent to Ukraine is on the rise, reaching 20,000 soldiers . The trend shows that Cuba could even surpass the number of troops coming from North Korea or failed African nations.

The young Cubans enlisted as Russian troops believed in promises of money and well-being for their families on the island. Instead, they have only found death, deception and dishonor. The Russian regime takes advantage of the need and desperation being experienced in Cuba and other countries. The offer includes $2,000 a month, Russian citizenship and 15 days of vacation every six months. It is an attractive promise that Putin has only half-fulfilled, generating desertions and discontent.

Russia is not winning the war, no matter how many churches, schools or civilian apartment buildings it bombs. In fact, it the day it invaded a sovereign country and decided to profit from poverty, recruiting soldiers through lies and false promises.

Russia’s strategy is illegal and criminal, yet unsurprising. Nevertheless, Latin American governments, with the support of the U.S., should join efforts to counter these deceptive Russian maneuvers and ensure that the Americas remain a free, prosperous and secure region for all.

Arturo McFields is an exiled journalist, former Nicaraguan ambassador to the Organization of American States, and a former member of the Norwegian Peace Corps. He is an alumnus of the National Defense University’s Security and Defense Seminar and the Harvard Leadership course.

articles.title: Impact of Dolly Parton's Imagination Library praised
articles.summary: The former Reading MP said he believed the town was the second place in the country to get books.
articles.body:
The impact of Dolly Parton's children's literary scheme has been praised by a former MP who helped bring the scheme to his constituency.

Tributes have been poured in for the country singer who died aged 80 . Her Imagination Library has had a presence across the South since it was launched in the UK in 2007.

Martin Salter, who was the MP for Reading West from 1997 until 2010, said he believed his constituency was the second place in the country to receive books.

Just over 3 million children are thought to have benefited from the scheme, which operates in the United States, UK, Australia, Canada and Ireland, with more than 330 million books distributed.

Salter said the aim of the scheme was the put books in homes where "reading was not the norm" and that Parton will be remembered in part for her "generosity and philanthropy".

Her programme was first launched in Sevier County, Tennessee, where the star grew up and was first inspired by her illiterate father.

Salter said it was a good tool in trying to normalise reading in homes where that might not have taken place otherwise.

He said: "In my time in public life in Reading, I've seen some pretty heart wrenching stuff – kids who are scared to bring homework home because their father can't read and doesn't want books in the house. What chance has a kid like that got?"

Children in Hampshire are amongst those who are current recipients of books from the Imagination Library, while other beneficiaries have lived in Blackbird Leys, Rose Hill, Berinsfield and Littlemore in Oxfordshire.

Colin Larkin, the founder and former editor of the Encyclopedia of Popular Music, who is from Poundbury, Dorset, said Parton's legacy as a performer is "remarkable".

He added: "She was the greatest country singer of all time. But beyond that she was an incredible icon. There's no dirt on her; there's no scandal. She had a marriage that lasted 60 years before her husband died last year.

"She had the persona of a dumb blonde – she was the absolute opposite of that. She was such a smart woman. She appealed to everybody - to women, in particular."

Her legacy will "unquestionably" continue, Larkin added.

"It's like The Beatles, an icon like that, that will go on and on."

articles.title: US halts immigrant visa applications for global ‘in-depth’ training course
articles.summary: The Trump administration has paused immigrant visa appointments worldwide to carry out “in-depth training” for consular officers to screen out foreign applicants at risk of taking advantage of U.S. public assistance. The guidance from the State Department comes after a federal judge last week vacated President Trump’s policy suspending visa processing from 75 countries whose…
articles.body:
The Trump administration has paused immigrant visa appointments worldwide to carry out “in-depth training” for consular officers to screen out foreign applicants at risk of taking advantage of U.S. public assistance.

The guidance from the State Department comes after a federal judge last week vacated President Trump’s policy suspending visa processing from 75 countries whose nationals the administration deemed likely to require public assistance.

“A more prosperous American means ensuring that visa applicants are not likely to become a public charge, as defined under U.S. law and regulation, and not likely to become dependent on U.S. public benefits reserved for qualified Americans in need,” a State Department spokesperson told The Hill in an email on Wednesday.

The spokesperson said that a global, in-depth training initiative was launched in early August at all U.S. embassies and consulates worldwide and that “appointments for visa and services will be adjusted.”

“Whenever there are changes to visa interview appointments, embassies and consulates communicate any changes directly to visa applicants,” the spokesperson said.

The pause on visa applications follows Trump’s hardline tack on immigration, where the administration has boasted about revoking more than 175,000 visas from individuals it said had violated the terms by committing criminal offenses, but that largely relied on encounters with law enforcement. The administration announced on Monday it was working to revoke short-term visas from individuals who used them to enter the U.S. and then file asylum claims, with some reports claiming the administration has a goal of canceling 200,000 visas.

The administration has also prioritized revoking visas and permanent residency, or green cards, from people who it deems are a threat to U.S. national security, but advocates say officials are targeting protected free speech like political opinions and pro-Palestinian protests.

But the Trump administration’s policy has received legal pushback. In a ruling on Friday, U.S. District Judge Jeannette Vargas, an appointee of former President Biden, said the Trump administration had exceeded its authority in pausing visa processing for 75 countries , saying a person’s nationality does not indicate they do not have the financial means to support themselves in the U.S.

The judge said that consular officers have the exclusive authority to evaluate visa applicants individually.

articles.title: Kinley Rasmus breaks LLWS hits record for a girl, a day after notching her second strikeout record
articles.summary: Kinley Rasmus continues to etch her name in the Little League World Series record book.
articles.body:
Kinley Rasmus continued her dominant run at the Little League World Series on Tuesday with another tournament record as her Phenix City, Alabama, team advanced from another elimination game.

A day after tying the total strikeouts records for a girl in the Little League World Series, Rasmus broke the tournament's record for most hits by a girl. She did so with a fifth-inning single that put runners on the corners in a 4-2 win for Phenix City over Tacoma, Washington.

The hit was Rasmus' fifth of the tournament to claim the record as her own. And Phenix City advanced while eliminating Tacoma.

On Monday, Rasmus made LLWS history on the mound — for the second time.

Rasmus struck out six to help lift Phenix City past West Chester, Pennsylvania, 6-5, in their elimination game Monday. The two-way star has compiled 14 total strikeouts in the tournament, which again matched Mo'ne Davis for the most strikeouts by a girl in tournament history.

Rasmus struck out eight in Phenix City's first game at the Little League World Series last week, which also tied a single-game record Davis set in 2014.

And thanks in part to Rasmus, Phenix City rallied out of a five-run hole on Monday night. Rasmus threw more than four scoreless innings after coming in for relief to help spark the rally. It marked the team's second straight elimination win.

Rasmus is the daughter of former MLB pitcher Cory Rasmus and the niece of former MLB outfielder Colby Rasmus . Cory is an assistant coach for Phenix City this summer, and both brothers played on Phenix City's 1999 Little League World Series team.

Rasmus is one of two girls playing in the tournament this year. Carsynn Meyer is playing for Paseo Verde (Nevada). They are among the 25 girls who have competed in the event's 79-year history.

While Phenix City can't lose again and advance, Rasmus has already put herself in elite LLWS company. She's one strikeout away from breaking Davis' record and may have another chance on the mound thanks to Tuesday's win.

Phenix City will next face Great Lakes winner Hamilton, Ohio, on Wednesday in another elimination game.
